content: The atrium, in anatomical terms, refers to a chamber or space within the body. It can describe the atrium of the lateral ventricle in the brain or, more commonly, the blood-collecting chamber of the heart. The atrium has a thin-walled structure that facilitates the return of blood to the heart. In animals with a closed circulatory system, there is at least one atrium. In fish, the circulatory system is relatively simple, consisting of a two-chambered heart with one atrium and one ventricle. In other vertebrates, the circulatory system is more complex, with either a three-chambered heart (two atria and one ventricle) or a four-chambered heart (two atria and two ventricles). The atrium receives blood returning to the heart to complete the circulatory cycle, while the ventricle pumps blood out of the heart to initiate a new cycle. Human Heart Humans have a four-chambered heart, which includes the right atrium, left atrium, right ventricle, and left ventricle. Right Atrium: The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from the superior vena cava and inferior vena cava. It sends this blood to the right ventricle, which then pumps it to the lungs for oxygenation. The right atrium does not have valves at its inlets, which allows for normal venous pulsation that can be detected in the jugular vein (e.g., jugular venous pressure). Internally, the right atrium contains rough pectinate muscles, the crista terminalis (a boundary within the atrium), and a smooth-walled part derived from the sinus venosus. Additionally, the interatrial septum contains the fossa ovalis, a remnant of the fetal foramen ovale, which bypassed the lungs during fetal development. Left Atrium: The left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the left and right pulmonary veins. It pumps this blood to the left ventricle, which then sends it to the aorta for distribution to the rest of the body. The left atrium forms the major component of the heart's base and has a slightly thicker wall than the right atrium. Its interior consists of a larger smooth-walled part, formed by the absorption of embryonic pulmonary veins, and a smaller muscular auricle with pectinate muscles, which is a remnant of the left part of the primordial atrium. Anatomy of the Atria Right Atrium The right atrium forms the right border of the heart. The superior vena cava and inferior vena cava drain systemic venous blood into the smooth posterior wall of the right atrium. The anterior wall of the right atrium is ridged and composed of pectinate muscles, creating a rough muscular surface. Right Auricle The right atrium contains a right auricle, a conical muscular pouch that overlaps the ascending aorta. The right auricle is an embryonic remnant that increases the capacity of the right atrium. Openings of the Superior and Inferior Vena Cava The superior vena cava opens into the superior part of the right atrium at the level of the right third costal cartilage. The inferior vena cava opens into the inferior part of the right atrium, nearly in line with the superior vena cava, at approximately the level of the fifth costal cartilage. Coronary Sinus The coronary sinus is a venous collection system that receives systemic blood from the cardiac veins at the posterior part of the coronary groove. It is derived from the embryonic venous sinus. The opening of the coronary sinus is located between the right atrioventricular orifice and the inferior vena cava orifice. Sinus Venarum The posterior part of the right atrium contains a smooth-walled pouch called the sinus venarum, which receives poorly oxygenated blood from the coronary sinus, superior vena cava, and inferior vena cava. The sinus venarum is formed by the incorporation of the embryonic venous sinus into the primordial atrium, providing additional capacity for the right atrium. The sinus venarum is separated from the primordial atrium by the sulcus terminalis externally and the crista terminalis internally. Fossa Ovalis The fossa ovalis is a depression in the interatrial septum. It is a remnant of the foramen ovale, a fetal physiological shunt that allowed oxygenated blood from the placenta to bypass the lungs and flow directly into the left atrium. The limbus of the fossa ovalis (annulus ovalis) is the prominent oval margin of the fossa ovalis. It is located on the medial wall of the right atrium and circumscribes the septum primum anteriorly, posteriorly, and superiorly. Left Atrium The left atrium forms the major component of the heart's base. The interatrial septum is part of the left atrial wall and runs posteriorly and to the right. The wall of the left atrium is slightly thicker than that of the right atrium. The interior of the left atrium consists of two main parts: A larger smooth-walled part, believed to be formed by the absorption of parts of embryonic pulmonary veins. A smaller muscular auricle with pectinate muscles, believed to be a remnant of the left part of the primordial atrium. Pulmonary Veins Blood enters the left atrium through four valveless pulmonary veins, arranged in two pairs (left and right), located on the posterior wall. Left Auricle Similar to the right atrium, the left atrium also contains a left auricle. Unlike the right auricle, which overlaps the ascending aorta, the left auricle forms the superior part of the left border of the heart and overlaps the pulmonary trunk. The left auricle is a small muscular region containing pectinate muscles internally. Left Atrio-Ventricular Orifice At the level of the left atrio-ventricular orifice, oxygenated blood received from the pulmonary veins exits the left atrium to enter the left ventricle.
